title: Dharmapala
hook: the Sri Lankan layman who campaigned to restore Bodh Gaya and spoke in Chicago

segments.voice: Yesterday, pressure and revival. Your line was revival. This week: Borobudur's mountain of stone, the climb to open sky, two streams meeting in Vietnam, the birthplace found, back to the tree at Bodh Gaya, and revival. Today, one man who tied those last threads together. Day eight hundred ninety-six.

A young man from Colombo, dressed in white, comes to Bodh Gaya on pilgrimage. He has read about this place: the tree, the seat of awakening. What he finds is a temple in poor repair, in the hands of others, with few Buddhists to be seen. By his own account, he sits near the tree and makes up his mind: he will give his life to bringing Buddhists back to this place. He has no title. He isn't a monk. He isn't a king. What he has is a voice, and he decides to use it. Today, the man who called himself Dharmapala.
screen: `A YOUNG MAN IN WHITE AT BODH GAYA.` → `A TEMPLE IN POOR REPAIR.` → `HE DECIDES TO USE HIS VOICE.`

segments.voice: First, the name and the white cloth. He was born into a Sri Lankan family and took the name Dharmapala, protector of the Dharma, along with the title Anagarika, one who has left home. He lived without marrying and gave himself to the teaching, but through his campaigning years he stayed a layman; he was ordained a monk only near the end of his life. Second, Bodh Gaya. The temple and its lands had long been held by a Hindu monastery, under its head, the mahant. Dharmapala wanted Buddhists to have a say at the place of awakening. He founded a society to work for it, wrote, petitioned, raised money, and went to court. He did not win in his lifetime. After his death, the law set up a committee of Hindus and Buddhists to care for the temple together. Both sides held the place dear, and the answer, in the end, was to share it. Third, Chicago. At a great gathering of the world's religions held in Chicago, he stood up and spoke for Buddhism to an American audience. Fourth, the whole man. His life wasn't simple. Some of his writing was hard, even harsh, toward other communities, and historians still argue over that part of his legacy. He's remembered with admiration and with argument, both. But the thread through all of it is clear: he loved something, and he wouldn't keep quiet about it.
screen: `ANAGARIKA: A LAYMAN WHO LEFT HOME.` · `A CAMPAIGN FOR BODH GAYA.` · `A BUDDHIST VOICE IN CHICAGO.` · `ADMIRED, AND ARGUED OVER.` · then, large: `HE SPOKE UP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: speak up for something you love. Settle and breathe. Choose one thing you care about that could use a voice: a place, a person, a practice, a cause. Now find one honest sentence you could say for it, out loud, to someone, this week. Keep it kind. Keep it true. Say it silently a few times and notice how it sits in your body. If it carries any heat or harshness, soften it, until it's a sentence you'd be glad to hear said about something you love. The bell holds the time.
Dharmapala. The Sri Lankan layman who campaigned for Buddhists at Bodh Gaya and spoke for the teaching in Chicago. Today's word.
Your line: he spoke up. Today, say your one honest sentence for something you love, kindly, to one person. Day eight hundred ninety-six.

howItsDone: Dharmapala is remembered in Sri Lanka and India as a Buddhist reformer, and the society he founded still works for Buddhist sites and pilgrims, while the Mahabodhi Temple at Bodh Gaya is cared for by a committee of Hindus and Buddhists.

fork.reveal: by his own account, he resolved there to give his life to it, and he spent it writing, petitioning, and speaking as a layman; he was ordained a monk only near the end of his life.

Audit: SERIOUS fix. The script said he 'stayed a layman, not a monk' and 'never' became one; Dharmapala took the novice robes in 1931 and higher ordination in 1933 at Sarnath, shortly before his death (as Devamitta Dhammapala). Teach, myth and fork reveal corrected. Confirm.
